| Long answer | 15 marks | 250 words | 12 to 13 minutes |
| Essay (per essay) | 125 marks | 1,000 to 1,200 words | 90 minutes |

Each GS paper has 20 questions in a 3-hour window, which works out to roughly 9 minutes per question. Practise under this constraint from Week 1 onward.

A strong GS answer has three parts:

1. Introduction: One or two sentences defining the context or stating the core issue.
2. Body: 3 to 5 points with examples, data, or case references. Two to three sentences per point.
3. Conclusion: A forward-looking observation or policy recommendation. Not a restatement of the introduction.

Diagrams help in GS I (maps, timelines) and GS III (data charts, infrastructure diagrams). A relevant diagram can replace 50 words and improve clarity.

---

## Choosing your Optional

To test whether a subject is workable, write 400 words on any topic from its syllabus without looking anything up. If you can do that now, it's a viable choice.

Among candidates who made the final merit list in 2023 and 2024, per UPSC's published mark sheets, Sociology, History, Public Administration, and Anthropology were chosen most frequently. These subjects have well-documented past papers and preparation material. That doesn't make them right for everyone. A subject you know well consistently outperforms one chosen for strategic reasons.

---

## Mistakes that cost marks

Underperformance in Mains often traces to preparation habits, not subject knowledge gaps.

- Starting a new Optional after Week 2 of preparation
- Spending more than 30 minutes per day on newspapers instead of writing answers
- Leaving Ethics theory for the final week
- Not timing essay practice
- Skipping sleep in the 3 days before each paper

---

## Frequently asked questions

### When does UPSC Mains 2026 start?

UPSC Civil Services Mains 2026 begins on August 21, 2026, per the official exam calendar published on upsc.gov.in.

### How many papers are in UPSC Mains?

UPSC Mains has 9 papers. Two are qualifying papers (Indian language and English, 300 marks each, with a 25% minimum required to pass). The remaining 7 count toward the merit list: Essay (250 marks), GS I through GS IV (250 marks each), and Optional Paper I and II (250 marks each). Total merit marks: 1,750.

### What are the total marks for UPSC Mains?

The written examination carries 1,750 marks across 7 merit papers. The personality test adds 275 marks, making the grand total 2,025. Language papers are qualifying only and not included in this count.

### How should I prepare for UPSC Mains in 9 weeks?

Divide the 9 weeks by subject: Weeks 2 and 3 for GS I and GS II, Weeks 4 and 5 for GS III and IV, Weeks 6 and 7 for Optional, Week 8 for Essay and current affairs, and Week 9 for revision and mock tests. Write answers daily from Week 1. Answer writing practice matters more than additional reading at this stage.

### Which Optional subject should I choose?

Choose the subject you know best and can write answers on from memory. Among candidates who made the 2023 and 2024 merit lists, per UPSC's published mark sheets, Sociology, History, Public Administration, and Anthropology were chosen most frequently. Familiarity with the subject matters more than its popularity.

---

## Quick reference

| Detail | Information |
|---|---|
| Mains start date | August 21, 2026 |
| Total merit papers | 7 |
| Total merit marks | 1,750 |
| Interview marks | 275 |
| Grand total | 2,025 |
| Official exam calendar | upsc.gov.in/examinations/exam-calendar |
| Admit card | upsc.gov.in (expected first week of August 2026) |

Roughly 10,000 to 13,000 candidates qualify for UPSC Mains each year, based on UPSC's published Prelims results from 2021 to 2024. With 933 vacancies in 2026, the written examination is where actual selection happens. What you write in those 5 days matters more than anything you read in the 64 days before them.

title: SSC Typing Test and DEST: Speed, Errors, and How to Pass
description: The SSC skill test carries no marks but eliminates candidates. Here are the real speed and error limits, and why the 35 WPM figure is often quoted wrong.
author: SarkariDarapan Team
content:
The SSC skill test is worth zero marks. It is also the last thing standing between a large number of candidates and a government post, every single cycle.

That combination is why it gets neglected. Candidates rank preparation by marks, the typing test carries none, so it drops to the bottom of the list and gets discovered late. Typing speed is a motor skill built over weeks. It cannot be acquired in the fortnight between a written result and a test date.

There is also a specific piece of misinformation about this test that circulates widely, and it is checkable with arithmetic. I will come to that.

## Two different tests that get confused

Most of the confusion in this area comes from treating the skill test as one thing. It is not.

The **Data Entry Speed Test**, or DEST, applies to SSC CGL and to Data Entry Operator posts. It measures **key depressions**, meaning individual keystrokes, over a set duration.

The **typing test** applies to CHSL posts such as Lower Division Clerk and Junior Secretariat Assistant, and to Postal Assistant. It measures **words per minute**.

Different tests, different units, different standards, different durations. Sites that publish one set of numbers under a heading covering both are describing two things at once, and that is where candidates pick up wrong targets.

## The real standards

| Test | Standard | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| CGL DEST | 8,000 key depressions per hour | 15 minutes |
| CHSL typing, English | 35 words per minute | 10 minutes |
| CHSL typing, Hindi | 30 words per minute | 10 minutes |
| DEO Grade A, CAG | 15,000 key depressions per hour | As notified |

Eight thousand key depressions per hour sounds abstract. Over a 15 minute test it means **2,000 key depressions**, which is the number you will actually be measured against.

## Why the 35 WPM figure for DEST is wrong

Several sites state that the CGL DEST works out to approximately 35 words per minute. That figure is incorrect, and you can verify it yourself in one step.

Two thousand key depressions over fifteen minutes is 133.3 key depressions per minute. The standard convention treats a word as five keystrokes. So 133.3 divided by 5 gives roughly **27 words per minute**, not 35.

The 35 WPM number belongs to the CHSL typing test, which is a different test with a different standard measured over ten minutes rather than fifteen. Sites covering both under one heading have carried the CHSL figure across to DEST.

This matters practically. A candidate targeting CGL who trains to 35 WPM is over-preparing on speed, which is harmless. A candidate who reads 35 WPM, decides the bar is far away, and gives up is being discouraged by a number that does not apply. And a candidate who assumes DEST and the CHSL typing test have the same standard will train for the wrong duration.

Train to comfortably clear the standard for the test you are actually sitting, and check the notification for your cycle rather than a blog table, including this one.

## The error limit almost nobody mentions

Here is the fact that surprises candidates most, and it changes preparation entirely.

The error tolerance is not the same for all posts.

| Post group | UR | OBC / EWS | SC / ST |
|---|---|---|---|
| General posts (LDC, JSA, DEO) | 20% | 25% | 30% |
| Tax Assistant and ASO | 5% | 7% | 7% |

Read those two rows again. A candidate sitting the test for Lower Division Clerk may make errors on up to 20 per cent of the material. A candidate sitting the same test for Tax Assistant may make errors on 5 per cent.

That is a four-fold stricter accuracy bar for the posts that pay more and attract stronger candidates. Persons with benchmark disabilities have separate limits, higher in both groups.

The consequence is that speed and accuracy training have to be balanced differently depending on the post you have applied to. For general posts, a candidate who types quickly with moderate accuracy will pass. For Tax Assistant or ASO, that same candidate fails, because 5 per cent is a demanding standard that requires deliberate accuracy work rather than raw speed.

Check which limit applies to the posts in your preference order. Candidates routinely train against the lenient figure and then sit the test for a post governed by the strict one.

## Which posts require which test

Knowing whether a skill test applies to you at all is the first question, and it depends on the posts in your preference order rather than on the examination you sat.

Within **SSC CGL**, the Data Entry Speed Test applies to Tax Assistant in the Central Excise and Income Tax departments, and to Assistant Section Officer in the Central Secretariat Service. Most other CGL posts do not carry a skill test, which is why many CGL candidates never encounter one.

Within **SSC CHSL**, the typing test applies to Lower Division Clerk, Junior Secretariat Assistant, and Postal Assistant and Sorting Assistant. The Data Entry Speed Test applies to Data Entry Operator posts. So essentially every CHSL candidate faces one or the other.

**Data Entry Operator Grade A** in the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General carries the highest standard at 15,000 key depressions per hour, roughly double the ordinary DEST requirement.

Several **Selection Post** positions carry typing or data entry requirements depending on the post, stated in the individual notification.

The practical implication is that your preference order determines your exposure. A CGL candidate who ranks Tax Assistant and ASO highly has committed to a strict-accuracy skill test. One who ranks Inspector and Assistant Audit Officer highly may face none at all. That is worth knowing before you submit preferences rather than after.

## What happens if you fail

Failing the skill test does not fail the whole recruitment in every case, and the outcome depends on your preference structure.

You become ineligible for the posts requiring the test. If your preference order also contains posts with no skill test requirement, and your rank reaches them, you can still be allotted one of those.

If every post you ranked requires the test, failing it ends the cycle for you regardless of your written performance.

Some cycles offer a re-test in defined circumstances, such as a technical failure at the centre, but a re-test on grounds of underperformance is not generally available.

That structure creates a specific planning implication. A candidate who is confident of their written performance but unsure of their typing might reasonably include some non-skill-test posts in the preference order as a floor, provided those posts are ones they would genuinely accept. Ranking a post purely as insurance, when you would decline it, creates its own problem since allotment is binding.

The better answer is to prepare the skill test properly so the question does not arise.

## Accuracy before speed, and why

Given the error limits, the training order matters and most candidates get it backwards.

Speed built on poor technique plateaus and then degrades under pressure. Accuracy built first supports speed that holds up on the day.

The mechanism is straightforward. Errors cost time twice: once to make and once to correct, if correction is even permitted in the format you are sitting. A typist at 40 WPM with 10 per cent errors is slower in effective terms than one at 32 WPM with 2 per cent errors, and on a strict-limit post the first one simply fails.

So the sequence is: learn correct finger placement, build accuracy at a comfortable pace, then increase speed while holding accuracy steady. If accuracy falls as speed rises, you have gone too fast and should drop back.

This takes weeks rather than days, which is the entire argument for starting before your written result rather than after it.

## Hindi typing and the layout question

Candidates opting for Hindi face a decision that English typists do not, and it needs making early.

Hindi typing uses different keyboard layouts, with the Krutidev and Mangal conventions being the ones that appear in government tests. They are not interchangeable. Muscle memory built on one does not transfer to the other, and switching late is genuinely difficult.

The notification specifies which layout applies. Read it before you begin practice, not after you have spent two months building the wrong muscle memory.

Hindi typing also carries a slightly lower speed standard for CHSL, 30 words per minute against 35 for English, which reflects the additional complexity of the script and the layout.

If you are equally comfortable in both languages, the practical consideration is which you can practise more effectively with the material available to you, since good Hindi typing practice material is less abundant online than English.

## What the test day actually looks like

The test is conducted on a computer at a designated centre, on the machine and keyboard provided rather than one you are used to.

That last point deserves attention. A candidate who has practised for months on their own laptop keyboard sits down at an unfamiliar keyboard with different key travel and spacing, and their speed drops. Practise on a standard external keyboard rather than only on a laptop, and if possible on more than one, so that the adjustment on the day is small.

A passage is displayed and you type it within the time limit. The system measures your key depressions or words per minute and your error rate against the passage.

There is generally no opportunity to review and polish at the end, so accuracy has to be maintained throughout rather than corrected afterwards.

Follow the instructions given at the centre precisely, including on backspacing and correction, since the rules on these affect how errors are counted and they are stated in the instructions rather than being universal.

## How to practise properly

Practise the actual format. Fifteen minutes for DEST, ten for the CHSL typing test. Practising in two minute bursts builds a different skill from sustaining accuracy across a full test, and the fatigue in the last third is where errors cluster.

Practise daily rather than in long weekly sessions. Motor skills consolidate with frequency, and fifteen minutes a day beats two hours on a Sunday.

Use passages similar to the exam material, which is ordinary prose rather than technical text or random words.

Measure honestly. Track both speed and error rate every session and record them, because a candidate who tracks only speed will not notice accuracy degrading as speed rises.

Set your training target above the standard, not at it. Nerves and an unfamiliar keyboard cost you something on the day, and a candidate sitting exactly at the standard in practice is at real risk.

Start now. If you are reading this before a written result, that is the correct time to begin.

## A twelve week plan from zero

For a candidate who does not touch-type at all, here is what a realistic build looks like. Compress it if you already type reasonably.

**Weeks one to three, technique only.** Learn correct finger placement on the home row and the reach patterns for every key. Type slowly and deliberately without looking at the keyboard. Speed during this phase is irrelevant and chasing it entrenches bad habits. Fifteen to twenty minutes daily.

**Weeks four to six, accuracy at a comfortable pace.** Continue without looking, working ordinary prose passages. The target is accuracy above 97 per cent at whatever speed that requires, even if it is slow. Begin recording speed and error rate each session so you have a baseline.

**Weeks seven to nine, speed with accuracy held.** Push pace gradually. The rule is that accuracy holds; whenever it drops, slow down until it recovers. This is where most of the speed gain happens, and it happens on the foundation built earlier rather than despite it.

**Weeks ten to twelve, exam conditions.** Full-duration practice, fifteen minutes for DEST or ten for the typing test, on a standard external keyboard, timed, scored honestly against the error limit that applies to your post. Two or three sessions a week at full duration plus shorter daily practice.

Throughout, track numbers rather than relying on impression. A simple log of date, speed and error rate shows whether you are improving or plateauing, and it removes the self-deception that comes from remembering good sessions and forgetting bad ones.

If you reach week twelve comfortably above the standard with accuracy well inside your error limit, you are ready. If you are sitting exactly at the standard, keep going, because the day costs you something.

## Why this stage catches out strong candidates

There is a pattern worth naming, because it explains why the failure rate at this stage is not concentrated among weak candidates.

Candidates who perform well in written examinations are, by selection, people who are good at studying. Studying rewards understanding, retention and analysis, and effort converts into marks in a way that feels proportionate.

Typing rewards none of those things. It is a motor skill, it improves through repetition rather than comprehension, and no amount of understanding how typing works makes you faster. A candidate who has succeeded through intellectual effort has no advantage here and may have a disadvantage, because the training feels unrewarding in a way studying does not.

The second factor is that the stage carries no marks. Candidates allocate effort by return, and a stage worth zero marks attracts zero effort until it becomes urgent.

The third is timing. The skill test arrives after a written result, at a point when a candidate feels the hard part is behind them, and the psychological shift from relief back to disciplined daily practice is genuinely difficult.

Recognising all three in advance is most of the fix. Treat the skill test as a separate project with its own schedule, started early and maintained regardless of where the written stages stand.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the SSC typing test qualifying or does it carry marks?**

Strictly qualifying. Your performance is not added to the merit list and a strong typing score improves your rank by nothing. But failing removes you from consideration for any post requiring it, regardless of your written performance, which is why the combination of zero marks and total elimination makes it the most neglected stage in SSC recruitment.

**What is the typing speed required for SSC CGL DEST?**

Eight thousand key depressions per hour, which over the 15 minute test means 2,000 key depressions. Working that through, 2,000 over 15 minutes is 133.3 per minute, and at the standard five keystrokes per word that is roughly 27 words per minute.

**Is SSC CGL DEST 35 words per minute?**

No, and this is a common error. The 35 WPM figure belongs to the CHSL typing test, which is a different test measured over ten minutes. The arithmetic on DEST gives roughly 27 WPM. Sites covering both tests under one heading have carried the CHSL number across to DEST.

**What is the typing speed for SSC CHSL?**

Thirty-five words per minute in English or thirty in Hindi, over a ten minute test. The lower Hindi standard reflects the additional complexity of the script and layout.

**How many errors are allowed in the SSC typing test?**

It depends on the post. For general posts such as LDC, JSA and DEO the limits are 20 per cent for UR, 25 for OBC and EWS, and 30 for SC and ST. For Tax Assistant and ASO the limits are far stricter at 5 per cent for UR and 7 per cent for other categories. Persons with benchmark disabilities have separate, higher limits.

**Why is the error limit stricter for Tax Assistant?**

Those posts involve data handling where accuracy carries direct consequences, and the recruitment sets the standard accordingly. The practical implication is that a candidate whose speed is fine but whose accuracy sits around 10 per cent will pass comfortably for LDC and fail for Tax Assistant on exactly the same performance.

**Should I practise speed or accuracy first?**

Accuracy. Errors cost time twice, to make and to correct, and speed built on poor technique degrades under pressure. Build accuracy at a comfortable pace, then raise speed while holding accuracy steady, dropping back whenever accuracy falls.

**Which Hindi keyboard layout does SSC use?**

The notification specifies it, and Krutidev and Mangal are the conventions that appear. They are not interchangeable and muscle memory does not transfer between them, so read the notification before beginning practice rather than after building the wrong habit.

**How long does it take to reach SSC typing speed?**

Weeks of daily practice for most candidates starting from ordinary keyboard familiarity, longer for those starting from scratch or working in Hindi with an unfamiliar layout. It cannot be compressed into the gap between a written result and a test date, which is the single most common reason candidates fail this stage.

**Can I use my own keyboard at the test centre?**

No. The test is conducted on the machine and keyboard provided, which is why practising only on a laptop is risky. Train on a standard external keyboard, and ideally on more than one, so the adjustment on the day is small rather than costly.

## Sources

- Staff Selection Commission: https://ssc.gov.in

The notification for your cycle is the authority on the speed standard, the error limit applicable to your post, the duration and the Hindi layout. SSC states these per recruitment and has varied them, so check the document rather than any summary table, this one included.

A closing thought. Every stage of SSC recruitment except this one rewards you in proportion to your effort. The typing test is pass or fail, it carries no marks, and thousands of candidates who cleared genuinely difficult written papers lose the post here. Fifteen minutes a day, starting now, is the whole solution.

title: How to Fill Government Job Applications Online - Step by Step
description: A detailed walkthrough for filling online government job application forms covering registration, document upload, fee payment, and common mistakes to avoid.
author: Mahitosh Dey
content:
## Why Filling Government Job Applications Correctly Matters

Every year, lakhs of candidates miss out on government job opportunities not because they lacked qualifications, but because they made errors in their application forms. A wrong photograph size, an incorrect date of birth, or a missed payment can lead to outright rejection, regardless of how well-prepared you are for the exam.

This comprehensive guide walks you through the entire process of filling online government job applications. Whether you are applying for SSC, UPSC, Railway, Banking, or any state-level exam, these steps and tips will help you submit error-free applications.

## Before You Start: Gather All Required Documents

Before sitting down to fill any government job application, make sure you have the following ready:

### Essential Documents (Digital Copies)

- **Passport-size photograph**: Recent, colored, white background, JPEG format, typically 20-50 KB, dimensions as specified (usually 3.5cm x 4.5cm at 100 DPI)
- **Signature scan**: Black ink on white paper, JPEG format, typically 10-20 KB
- **Aadhaar Card**: For identity verification and address proof
- **Educational Certificates**: 10th, 12th, Graduation, Post-graduation mark sheets and certificates
- **Caste/Category Certificate**: SC/ST/OBC/EWS certificate from the competent authority (if applicable)
- **Domicile Certificate**: State domicile or residential proof (for state-level posts)
- **Experience Certificate**: If experience is required for the post
- **Disability Certificate**: For PwBD candidates (if applicable)

### Important Personal Details

- Valid email ID (preferably Gmail)
- Active mobile number (that you will keep active for at least 1 year)
- Bank account details (for fee payment through net banking/UPI)
- Debit/Credit card details (if paying through card)

## Step-by-Step Application Process

### Step 1: Registration (One-Time)

Most government recruitment portals require one-time registration before you can apply for specific posts.

1. Visit the official recruitment website (e.g., ssc.gov.in, upsc.gov.in, rfrb.org.in)
2. Click on **"New Registration"** or **"Register"**
3. Enter your basic details: Full Name (as in 10th certificate), Father's Name, Mother's Name, Date of Birth, Gender, Mobile Number, Email ID
4. Create a strong password with at least 8 characters including uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and special characters
5. Verify your mobile number and email through OTP
6. Note down your **Registration Number/ID** and password securely

### Step 2: Login and Select the Post

1. Login to the portal using your Registration Number and password
2. Navigate to the **"Apply Online"** or **"Latest Notifications"** section
3. Read the official notification thoroughly before clicking apply
4. Click on **"Apply"** for the desired post

### Step 3: Fill Personal Details

This is the most critical section. Double-check every entry:

- **Full Name**: Exactly as printed on your 10th class certificate. Do not use nicknames or abbreviations
- **Father's/Mother's Name**: As on official documents
- **Date of Birth**: Match it with your 10th certificate, not Aadhaar (in case of discrepancy, 10th certificate is the standard)
- **Gender**: Male/Female/Transgender
- **Category**: General/OBC/SC/ST/EWS - Select the correct category as per your certificate
- **Nationality**: Indian
- **Marital Status**: As applicable
- **Address**: Current and permanent address with correct PIN code
- **Educational Qualification**: Enter details of all qualifications starting from 10th standard
- **Email and Mobile**: Provide active contact details

### Step 4: Upload Photographs and Documents

Document upload is where most candidates make mistakes. Follow these guidelines:

**Photograph Requirements (Typical)**:
- Format: JPEG/JPG only
- Size: Between 20 KB and 50 KB (varies by organization)
- Dimensions: 200 x 230 pixels or as specified
- Background: White or light-colored
- Recency: Taken within the last 3 months
- Attire: Formal, without sunglasses or cap (unless religious headgear)

**Signature Requirements (Typical)**:
- Sign with black ink pen on white paper
- Scan or photograph it clearly
- Format: JPEG/JPG
- Size: Between 10 KB and 20 KB
- Dimensions: 140 x 60 pixels or as specified

**Tips for Perfect Photo and Signature Scans**:
- Use a scanner app on your smartphone (like CamScanner or Adobe Scan)
- Crop tightly around the photo/signature
- Use an image resizing tool to get exact dimensions
- Compress if file size exceeds the limit (use tinyjpg.com or similar)
- Always preview the uploaded image before proceeding

### Step 5: Select Exam Center Preferences

- Choose 3-4 exam center preferences based on proximity to your location
- Popular centers fill up fast, so apply early
- Consider travel time, accommodation availability, and familiarity with the city
- Some exams allow center changes later, but do not rely on this

### Step 6: Pay the Application Fee

Most government exams charge an application fee (often with exemptions for SC/ST/PwBD/Female candidates):

**Payment Methods Available**:
- **Net Banking**: Using any nationalized or private bank
- **Debit Card**: Visa/Mastercard/Rupay
- **Credit Card**: Visa/Mastercard
- **UPI**: PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm, BHIM
- **Challan**: Some organizations offer offline payment through bank challans (SBI e-challan is common)

**Fee Payment Tips**:
- Pay within the deadline; late fees are rarely accepted
- Take a screenshot of the payment confirmation screen
- Save the transaction ID/reference number
- If payment is deducted but status shows "pending," wait 24-48 hours before retrying
- Never pay twice without confirming the first transaction failed
- Download the payment receipt/confirmation email

### Step 7: Review and Submit

This is your final chance to catch errors:

1. Review every section of the application form carefully
2. Preview the uploaded photograph and signature
3. Verify your exam center preferences
4. Check fee payment status shows "Success" or "Completed"
5. Click **"Final Submit"** only when everything is correct
6. Once submitted, most forms cannot be edited (some allow correction windows)

### Step 8: Download and Print Confirmation

- Download the **application form PDF** and save it on your computer and phone
- Take a printout and keep it safely until the recruitment process is complete
- Note the **Application Number/Roll Number** for future reference
- You will need this for downloading admit cards, checking results, etc.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

### Mistake 1: Name Mismatch

Ensure your name is exactly as on your 10th certificate across all documents. Even minor variations like "Raj Kumar" vs "Rajkumar" can cause issues during document verification.

### Mistake 2: Wrong Category Selection

Selecting a wrong category (e.g., General instead of OBC) can disqualify you during verification. Double-check your category certificate validity and the issuing authority.

### Mistake 3: Uploading Wrong Photo/Signature

An unclear photo, wrong dimensions, or signature in pencil can lead to rejection. Always follow the exact specifications mentioned in the notification.

### Mistake 4: Missing the Deadline

Government application deadlines are strict. Most portals close at 11:59 PM on the last date, and servers are overloaded in the final hours. Apply at least 3-5 days before the deadline.

### Mistake 5: Not Saving the Confirmation

If you lose your application number and did not save the confirmation page, recovering your application can be extremely difficult.

## Pro Tips for Government Job Applicants

1. **Create a dedicated email** for government job applications to keep all notifications in one place
2. **Maintain a document folder** on your phone and computer with all certificates pre-scanned in various sizes
3. **Apply early** in the application window to avoid last-minute technical glitches
4. **Read the notification PDF** completely before starting the form, especially eligibility conditions and reservation details
5. **Keep your Aadhaar updated** with current mobile number and address
6. **Track all applications** in a spreadsheet with application numbers, dates, fee status, and exam dates
7. **Set reminders** for admit card release dates and exam dates

## What to Do After Submitting the Application

After successful submission, stay alert for these milestones:

- **Correction Window**: Some organizations provide a 3-5 day window to correct application errors. Do not miss this
- **Admit Card Release**: Download it as soon as it is released and verify all details
- **Exam Day Preparation**: Carry your admit card, valid photo ID, and any other documents mentioned in the admit card instructions
- **Result and Cut-off**: Check the official website regularly after the exam

Filling government job applications may seem tedious, but getting it right the first time saves you from unnecessary hassle and ensures your candidacy is not rejected on technical grounds. Bookmark this guide and refer to it every time you apply for a new government job.

## Frequently asked questions

**What documents do I need before starting an online government job application?**

A scanned photograph and signature meeting the stated dimensions and file size, your Class 10 certificate for date of birth, degree and mark sheets, a category certificate in the prescribed format where applicable, and identity proof. Prepare all of these before opening the form rather than during it, because sessions time out and specification mismatches are the most common cause of rejection.

**Why does my photograph keep getting rejected?**

Almost always a specification mismatch: wrong dimensions, wrong file size, wrong format, or a background that does not meet the requirement. Some recruitments additionally require the photograph to show your name and the date. Read the exact specification in the notification rather than assuming a standard passport photograph will pass, since requirements differ between recruiting bodies.

**What happens if I make a mistake in my application?**

It depends on whether a correction window exists. Many recruitments open one for a short period after the application deadline, and it is the only opportunity to fix errors. Some fields are never editable, including category and sometimes the examination centre. Errors discovered after the correction window closes generally surface at document verification, where they can end the candidature.

**Is my application complete once I submit the form?**

Not until the fee payment succeeds. A submitted form with a failed or pending payment is not a valid application, and candidates lose cycles to this every year. Confirm the transaction, save the payment receipt, and check that your application status shows as complete rather than assuming submission was enough.

**Should I use my own email and mobile number?**

Yes, and one you will still control for the length of the process. Recruitments run for months and every communication including the admit card depends on that login. Using an agent's or a cyber cafe's contact details means losing access to your own candidature, which is a genuinely serious problem to unwind.

**Why should I not apply on the last day?**

Portals slow badly under load near deadlines and payment gateways fail. A failed payment on the final evening cannot be retried after the window closes, and no recruiting body extends a deadline for an individual candidate. Applying several days early costs nothing and removes the single most avoidable failure in the process.

**What is One Time Registration and do I need it?**

Several bodies including SSC and Kerala PSC use a one-time registration that creates a permanent profile, so you enter personal and educational details once and then apply to individual notifications with a few clicks. Set it up before a notification you care about opens, and keep it current, because an outdated profile can block applications without explaining why.

**How do I know my application was accepted?**

Check the application status on the portal rather than relying on a confirmation email, which may not arrive. Save or print the completed application and the fee receipt. Keep both until the recruitment concludes, since they are the evidence if a discrepancy arises later.

**Can someone else fill the form for me?**

It is legal but unwise. The details entered become your official record, errors made by someone else are still your problem at verification, and handing over your credentials means losing control of your candidature. If someone does assist, sit with them, check every field before submission, and keep the login details yourself.

**What should I do after submitting the application?**

Save the application printout and fee receipt, note the expected admit card window, and keep your login credentials somewhere durable. Then watch the official portal on a fixed schedule, because recruiting bodies publish admit cards and notices without individually notifying candidates.

title: Government Jobs vs Private Jobs in India 2026: Salary, Security
description: Government job or private job in India? An honest 2026 comparison across salary, security, perks, pension, work-life balance, and career growth to decide.
author: Mahitosh Dey
content:
---

Ask any Indian family about career advice and within five minutes someone will say it, *"Beta, sarkari naukri dekho."*

It is practically a cultural reflex. But is the advice any good today? On the other side, the private sector crowd will tell you government jobs are for people who cannot handle real competition.

Both sides are wrong, and both sides have a point.

The truth is that neither is universally better. What matters is what *you* want from your career and your life. To figure that out you need an honest comparison, not propaganda from either camp.

So here it is. Government jobs vs private jobs in India, broken down across every dimension that matters.

---

## 1. Salary: who really pays more?

This one surprises people.

Starting salary in most government jobs is lower than comparable private sector roles. An SSC CGL joiner starts at around Rs. 25,500 per month. A fresh engineering graduate at a mid-sized IT company in Pune starts at Rs. 30,000 to Rs. 45,000.

That is only the starting point. Here is where it gets interesting.

### Government salary: what you really take home

Government salaries under the 7th Pay Commission include Basic Pay (the official figure), Dearness Allowance (currently over 50% of basic pay, revised twice a year), House Rent Allowance (8% to 27% of basic pay depending on city), Transport Allowance, Medical Allowance, and other special allowances depending on department and posting.

A Level 7 government employee (like an Income Tax Inspector) with 10 years of service can easily be taking home Rs. 70,000 to Rs. 90,000 per month in a metro city, with a pension waiting at the end.

### Private sector salary: the high-growth reality

Private sector salaries are not equal. A software engineer at a top product company earns Rs. 20 to Rs. 50 lakh per year within 5 to 7 years. A mid-level manager at an MNC earns Rs. 15 to Rs. 25 lakh. But a teacher at a private school earns Rs. 15,000 to Rs. 25,000 per month with no benefits.

The private sector has a much wider range. The ceiling is higher, but so is the floor.

### Honest verdict

| | Government | Private |
|--|------------|---------|
| Starting pay | Lower to moderate | Moderate to high (varies widely) |
| Salary growth | Slow but steady (Pay Commission) | Fast in good sectors, stagnant in bad ones |
| In-hand after 10 years | Solid and predictable | Depends on industry, company, performance |
| Ceiling | Capped by Pay Matrix | Virtually unlimited in top sectors |

If you are going into IT, finance, or consulting, private pays more over a career. If you are going into teaching, administration, or non-technical roles, government often pays more in real terms once allowances are factored in.

---

## 2. Job security: the biggest difference

Let us be honest. This is where government jobs win, and it is not even close.

Once you are a confirmed government employee, removing you from service requires a formal departmental inquiry, due process, and in most cases approval from senior authorities. In practice, government employees almost never lose their jobs involuntarily outside of a serious misconduct.

Private sector employees can be, and regularly are, laid off at scale. In 2022 to 2024, some of the biggest names in tech globally laid off tens of thousands of employees in a single announcement. In India, IT layoffs, BPO shutdowns, and startup collapses have become routine news.

This is not a flaw in the private sector. It is how market-driven companies respond to downturns. But it is a reality you need to accept when you choose that path.

If job security matters to you, for your family, your loan EMIs, or simply your peace of mind, the government sector has an advantage that no private company can genuinely replicate.

---

## 3. Perks and benefits: government's hidden advantage

Salary numbers alone do not tell the full story. Government jobs come with a benefits package that most private companies simply cannot match.

### What government employees get

Government employees receive a guaranteed monthly pension for life after retirement (worth lakhs over a retired person's lifetime; NPS applies to newer recruits but OPS is still available for some roles). They also get a General Provident Fund where the government contributes on top of employee contribution and interest is tax-free.

Medical benefits under CGHS (Central Government Health Scheme) cover the employee and the entire family for life, including after retirement. Housing comes as government quarters in many cities at subsidised rent, or HRA if quarters are unavailable.

Leave is generous and protected: casual leave, earned leave, medical leave, maternity or paternity leave, and study leave are all available and usable without losing your job. Children's education allowance reimburses school fees. Leave Travel Concession covers family travel costs every 4 years to anywhere in India. Railway employees also get free or heavily subsidised travel for the entire family. Gratuity is paid on retirement or resignation after 5 or more years.

### What private sector gives

Good private companies offer PF contribution, health insurance (usually Rs. 3 to 5 lakh for the employee), and sometimes a flexi-benefits allowance. Top MNCs add ESOPs, performance bonuses, and global exposure.

But the pension is almost always missing. Most private sector employees retire with whatever they have saved in PF and personal investments, which requires active discipline throughout a career.

| Benefit | Government | Private |
|---------|------------|---------|
| Pension | Yes (guaranteed for older employees, NPS for newer) | Rarely |
| Medical (family) | CGHS, lifelong | Usually employee-only, limited |
| Housing | Government quarters or HRA | HRA in salary, no quarters |
| Leave | Generous and protected | Varies, often pressured not to take |
| Children's education | Reimbursement available | Rare |
| Gratuity | Yes | Yes (if 5+ years) |
| Job security | Very high | Low to moderate |

---

## 4. Work-life balance: it depends on the job

Here is where the government job myth gets complicated.

The popular image of a government employee leaving office at 5 PM sharp is true *in some departments*. But it is not universal. A new IAS officer during a flood, a doctor in a government hospital, or an income tax officer during March closing are brutal jobs with long hours and real pressure.

On average, government jobs have fixed working hours (typically 9 AM to 5:30 PM), gazetted holidays, and genuine leave that you can take without your boss making you feel guilty. Weekends are mostly protected. There is no expectation of being available at 11 PM on WhatsApp.

Private sector jobs, especially in IT services, banking, startups, and consulting, routinely expect availability beyond office hours. Crunch time, weekend deployments, and late-night calls with clients in different time zones are common. The culture of being constantly available is real and exhausting for many people.

If you value your evenings, your weekends, and your ability to take a two-week vacation without your inbox exploding, government jobs generally offer a more protected personal life.

---

## 5. Career growth: private wins on speed

This is where the private sector has a clear and honest advantage.

In government, promotions are largely seniority-based. You wait your turn. A brilliant 25-year-old and a mediocre 40-year-old in the same grade get promoted at roughly the same time. Performance matters, but it rarely accelerates timelines dramatically.

In the private sector, a high performer can go from junior executive to senior manager in 4 to 5 years. A talented engineer can become a team lead, then an architect, then a VP of Engineering purely on merit. There is no queue.

The other side matters too. Private sector growth also has a brutal downside. You can be stuck in the same role for 5 years if your company stagnates, if your manager does not like you, or if the industry goes through a downturn. Government growth is slow but *guaranteed*. Private growth is fast but *not guaranteed*.

| | Government | Private |
|--|------------|---------|
| Promotion speed | Slow, seniority-based | Fast, merit-based |
| Ceiling | Pay Matrix cap | Virtually unlimited |
| Performance impact | Limited | Very high |
| Lateral moves | Rare | Common |
| Global exposure | Limited (mostly IFS) | High in MNCs |

---

## 6. Social status in India: still real, still matters

This might sound superficial, but in India it genuinely affects everyday life.

An IAS officer, a bank manager, a government doctor. These carry social weight that is hard to quantify but impossible to ignore. Rishte (marriage alliances), respect in the community, ease of getting a home loan, behaviour of local authorities. All of these are tangibly different for a government employee versus a private sector worker of similar income.

In urban metros, this gap has narrowed significantly. A software engineer at Google is socially as respected as an SSC officer. But in smaller cities and rural India, sarkari naukri still commands a level of respect and trust that private employment does not.

This is not something to be dismissive of. For many families it directly impacts life decisions, including marriage.

---

## 7. Stress and work culture: honest comparison

Government work culture has its own brand of stress. Bureaucratic slow-moving systems, political interference in some departments, frustration at the pace of decision-making, and limited ability to innovate or change things quickly. Transfers can disrupt family life significantly, especially in All India Services.

Private sector stress is different. It is deadline-driven, target-driven, and sometimes just exhausting. The always-on culture, performance reviews, quarterly targets, and the fear of being let go create a different but equally real kind of pressure.

Neither is stress-free. The type of stress is different. Pick the one you are better equipped to handle.

---

## 8. Which one is right for you?

Here is the honest answer. It depends on your values, not just your ambitions.

Choose government if security and stability matter more to you than high earnings, if you want a job that will not disappear when the market crashes, if your family depends on predictable income (EMIs, parents' health, etc.), if you value work-life boundaries and protected personal time, if you want to serve the public in a direct meaningful way, and if retirement security (pension) is important to you.

Choose private if you are in a high-growth field (tech, finance, consulting, management), if you are comfortable with risk in exchange for higher rewards, if you want fast career progression based purely on performance, if you thrive in dynamic fast-paced environments, if you want global exposure and opportunities abroad, and if you have the discipline to build your own retirement corpus.

The worst reason to choose government is because the exam is easy and you have no other plan. The worst reason to choose private is because it pays more starting out and government seems boring.

Both require a real choice, made with full awareness of what you are signing up for.

---

## The myth worth busting

People often frame this as a binary. Either you are a government employee, or you are in private. But life is messier than that.

Many people start in private, build skills, save aggressively, and then clear a government exam in their late 20s. Others spend 5 years in government, realise it is not for them, and move to the private sector using their administrative experience. Some run a small business alongside a government job (where rules permit).

The decision is not permanent and it is not life-defining. It is just a direction, and directions can change.

---

## Final scorecard

| Factor | Government | Private | Winner |
|--------|------------|---------|--------|
| Job security | Very high | Low to medium | Government |
| Starting salary | Moderate | Moderate to high | Private |
| Long-term earnings | Steady | High potential | Private (top fields) |
| Benefits and perks | Excellent | Good (varies) | Government |
| Pension | Yes | Rarely | Government |
| Work-life balance | Generally better | Often poor | Government |
| Career growth speed | Slow | Fast | Private |
| Social status | High (especially small cities) | Growing in metros | Depends |
| Innovation and learning | Limited | High | Private |
| Stress type | Bureaucratic | Performance-driven | Depends |

---

There is no universal winner. There is only the right choice for your situation, your values, and your appetite for risk.

If you are leaning towards government, start preparing now. Notifications do not wait, and the competition is serious. If you are leaning private, build your skills aggressively, save early, and do not ignore retirement planning just because there is no pension.

Whatever you choose, choose it deliberately. Not because your family pressured you, and not because your friends did. Because *you* decided this is what fits your life.

---

## Frequently asked questions

**Is a government job in India really better than a private job in 2026?**
Neither is universally better in 2026. Government jobs offer higher security, pension, CGHS medical coverage for the whole family for life, and better work-life balance. Private jobs in high-growth fields (IT, finance, consulting) pay more over a career and offer faster promotion. The right choice depends on your risk appetite and career field.

**What is the actual take-home difference between a government and private job after 10 years?**
A Level 7 central government employee (like an Income Tax Inspector) with 10 years of service takes home roughly Rs. 70,000 to Rs. 90,000 per month in a metro city, plus a pension after retirement. A software engineer at a top private product company can earn Rs. 20 to Rs. 50 lakh per year in the same 5-to-7-year window, but a private school teacher earns Rs. 15,000 to Rs. 25,000 per month with no benefits. Private has a wider range in both directions.

**Do government employees still get a pension in 2026?**
Older government recruits (joined before 1 January 2004 in central service, dates vary by state) receive the Old Pension Scheme (OPS) with a guaranteed monthly pension for life. Newer recruits are under the National Pension System (NPS), where the government contributes 14% and the employee contributes 10% to a market-linked corpus. NPS is less generous than OPS but still substantially better than private sector retirement provision, which is typically only PF and personal savings.

**How much job security does the private sector really offer in India?**
Private sector job security in India in 2026 is moderate at best. Confirmed government employees are almost impossible to remove without formal departmental inquiry and due process. Private sector employees can be laid off during quarterly earnings misses, industry downturns, or company restructuring. Indian tech, BPO, and startup layoffs across 2022 to 2024 affected tens of thousands of workers.

**Which sector gives better work-life balance in India?**
Government jobs generally offer better work-life balance across most departments, with fixed 9 AM to 5:30 PM hours, gazetted holidays, and protected weekends. Exceptions include IAS/IPS during crises, doctors in government hospitals, and revenue officers during year-end. Private sector, especially in IT services, banking, consulting, and startups, routinely expects availability beyond office hours and on weekends.

**Is CGHS medical coverage really that valuable?**
CGHS covers the government employee, spouse, dependent children, and dependent parents for life, including after the employee retires. Coverage includes outpatient consultations, hospitalisation at empanelled hospitals, and cashless treatment at CGHS wellness centres. A comparable private family floater plan for the same coverage across a 30-year career and retirement would cost lakhs in premium and often deny pre-existing conditions. CGHS is one of the most underrated government perks.

**Can I switch from government to private (or vice versa) later?**
Yes, both directions are possible and common. Private-to-government requires clearing a competitive exam, which is easier if you are under 30 (age limits vary by exam). Government-to-private is possible if you resign; some senior government officers move to consulting, corporate governance, or advisory roles after retirement. However, mid-career switches in either direction reset your seniority and can involve pay cuts initially.

**Which is a better choice for someone from a middle-class family?**
For a middle-class family in India, government jobs remain the safer choice because of predictable income for EMIs, protected medical costs for parents through CGHS, and pension for old age. Private sector makes sense if the individual has strong marketable skills (engineering, MBA from a top college, finance certifications), lives in a metro with good job market depth, and has the discipline to save 20-30% of income for retirement independently.

title: PM Kisan Samman Nidhi - How to Apply, Check Status & Fix Errors
description: Practical guide for PM Kisan Yojana covering new registration, eKYC, installment status check, and how to fix common problems like payment failures and name.
author: Mahitosh Dey
content:
## What is PM Kisan Samman Nidhi?

Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi, commonly called PM Kisan, is one of the most important government schemes for farmers in India. Under this scheme, eligible farmer families receive **Rs. 6,000 per year** in three installments of Rs. 2,000 each, directly deposited into their bank accounts. The scheme was launched in February 2019 and has since benefited over 11 crore farmer families across the country.

What makes PM Kisan different from many other government schemes is that the money goes **directly to the farmer's bank account** — there are no middlemen, no agents, and no commissions. If you are a farmer or someone in your family is, this guide will help you register, check your payment status, complete eKYC, and fix common problems.

For a broader overview of the scheme, you can also read our [complete PM Kisan Yojana guide](/blog/complete-guide-to-pm-kisan-yojana).

## How to Apply

There are three ways to register for PM Kisan. Choose the one that works best for you.

### Method 1: Online Registration (Self)

This is the fastest way to apply if you have internet access and basic smartphone or computer skills.

1. Open your browser and go to **pmkisan.gov.in**
2. Click on **"New Farmer Registration"** on the homepage
3. Select **"Rural Farmer Registration"** or **"Urban Farmer Registration"** based on your area
4. Enter your **Aadhaar number** and select your **state**
5. Enter the CAPTCHA code and click **"Search"**
6. If you are not already registered, you will see the registration form
7. Fill in your **name** (exactly as on Aadhaar), **gender**, **category** (SC/ST/General/OBC)
8. Enter your **bank account number**, **IFSC code**, and confirm the account number
9. Enter your **land details** — survey number, Khasra number, Khata number, and the area of land in hectares
10. Upload your **Aadhaar card** and **land documents** if required by your state
11. Submit the form and note down the **registration reference number**

### Method 2: Through Common Service Centre (CSC)

If you find the online process difficult, visit your nearest CSC:

1. Find a **Common Service Centre** in your village or nearby town
2. Carry your **Aadhaar card**, **bank passbook**, and **land documents** (Khatauni/Khasra)
3. Tell the CSC operator you want to register for PM Kisan
4. The operator will fill the form on your behalf and take your **biometric verification** (fingerprint)
5. You will get a registration slip — keep it safe

**CSC charges**: The CSC may charge a nominal service fee of Rs. 10-30 for the registration. This is not an official fee but is allowed for the operator's service.

### Method 3: Offline Through Patwari or Agriculture Office

In some states, the local Patwari or Lekhpal collects farmer details and submits them to the block agriculture office:

1. Contact your **village Pradhan**, **Patwari**, or **Block Agriculture Officer**
2. Submit copies of your Aadhaar card, bank passbook, and land documents
3. The official will add your details to the PM Kisan database
4. You can check your registration status online after 2-3 weeks

## How to Complete eKYC

eKYC is **mandatory** for all PM Kisan beneficiaries. Without it, your installments will stop. Here is how to do it:

### Online eKYC (OTP-Based)

1. Go to **pmkisan.gov.in**
2. Click on **"eKYC"** in the top menu bar
3. Enter your **Aadhaar number** and click **"Search"**
4. Your name and registration details will appear
5. Click **"Get OTP"** — an OTP will be sent to your Aadhaar-linked mobile number
6. Enter the OTP and click **"Submit"**
7. Your eKYC is now complete. You will see a confirmation message

**Important**: This method only works if your mobile number is linked to your Aadhaar. If it is not, you will need biometric eKYC.

### Biometric eKYC (at CSC)

1. Visit your nearest **Common Service Centre**
2. Carry your **Aadhaar card**
3. The CSC operator will use a biometric device to scan your **fingerprint**
4. Your fingerprint will be matched with your Aadhaar database
5. Once verified, your eKYC is complete

Biometric eKYC is the backup option when OTP-based eKYC fails. It is also more secure since it uses your fingerprint directly.

## How to Check PM Kisan Payment Status

### Method 1: Beneficiary Status on the Website

1. Visit **pmkisan.gov.in**
2. Click on **"Beneficiary Status"**
3. Enter your **Aadhaar number**, **account number**, or **mobile number**
4. Click **"Get Data"**
5. You will see a table showing all installments with dates and amounts

### Method 2: Through the PM Kisan Mobile App

1. Download the **PM Kisan Mobile App** from Google Play Store
2. Open the app and tap **"Check Beneficiary Status"**
3. Enter your Aadhaar number or mobile number
4. Your installment history will be displayed

### Method 3: Helpline Number

Call the PM Kisan helpline at **155261** or **011-24300606** (Monday to Friday, 9:30 AM to 6:00 PM).

### Understanding Status Terms

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| FTO is Generated and Payment confirmed | Payment successful, money has been sent to your bank |
| Rft Signed by State | State has approved your payment, waiting for central processing |
| Pending for approval at State/District | Your details are under verification at the state or district level |
| Aadhaar Authentication Failed | Your Aadhaar number does not match bank records |
| Account Number / IFSC Incorrect | Your bank details in PM Kisan records are wrong |

## How to Fix Common Errors

### Error 1: Aadhaar Authentication Failed

**Cause**: Your name in Aadhaar does not match the name in PM Kisan records, or your Aadhaar is not seeded with your bank account.

**Fix**: Visit your bank and get Aadhaar seeding done. Make sure the name in your bank account, Aadhaar card, and PM Kisan registration are all the same. If there is a spelling difference, get it corrected at the Aadhaar centre first.

### Error 2: Bank Account Validation Failed

**Cause**: Incorrect account number, wrong IFSC code, or closed bank account.

**Fix**: Log in to pmkisan.gov.in, go to **"Updation of Self Registered Farmer"**, and update your bank details. If the account is closed, open a new one and update the details. Make sure the IFSC code matches your specific branch.

### Error 3: Payment Status Shows Pending for Months

**Cause**: Your state government has not verified your land records yet, or there is a data mismatch.

**Fix**: Contact your **Block Agriculture Officer** or **District Agriculture Officer**. Ask them to check your record in the PM Kisan dashboard. They can approve pending applications or flag issues that need correction.

### Error 4: Name Mismatch Between Documents

**Cause**: Your name is spelled differently in Aadhaar, bank account, and land records. For example, "Ram Prasad" in Aadhaar and "Ramprasad" in the bank.

**Fix**: Get the name corrected in whichever document has the error. It is easiest to correct the Aadhaar name (visit an Aadhaar centre) or the bank name (visit your bank branch with ID proof). All three should match exactly.

### Error 5: Double Registration in Family

**Cause**: Both husband and wife registered separately, or a duplicate registration exists.

**Fix**: Only one member per family can be a beneficiary. If both have registered, the duplicate entry needs to be deleted. Contact your local agriculture office to remove the extra registration. The person whose name is on the land records should remain as the beneficiary.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How can I check my PM Kisan payment status online?

Visit pmkisan.gov.in, click on "Beneficiary Status" in the top menu, enter your Aadhaar number or account number or mobile number, and click "Get Data". You will see all your installment details including the amount, date, and status of each payment. The status will show as "FTO is Generated and Payment confirmed" if the payment was successful, or "Pending" if it is still being processed.

### My PM Kisan payment failed. How do I fix it?

Payment failures usually happen because of incorrect bank details, inactive Aadhaar seeding, or incomplete eKYC. First, check if your bank account is linked to your Aadhaar (visit your bank for Aadhaar seeding). Then complete your eKYC on pmkisan.gov.in. If your name in Aadhaar does not match your bank records, get it corrected. After fixing the issue, your pending payment will be released in the next cycle automatically.

### Can I register for PM Kisan without land in my name?

No, you generally cannot register if the land is not in your name. PM Kisan requires land ownership records that match the applicant's name. However, in some states, land can be in the joint name of family members. If the land is in your father's or spouse's name, the registration should be in their name, not yours. Check your state's specific rules, as some states have provisions for tenant farmers.

### Is eKYC mandatory for PM Kisan beneficiaries?

Yes, eKYC is mandatory for all PM Kisan beneficiaries. Without completing eKYC, your installments will be held and you will not receive any new payments. You can complete eKYC online through the PM Kisan portal using your Aadhaar-linked mobile number for OTP verification, or you can visit a Common Service Centre (CSC) for biometric eKYC using fingerprint. Complete it as soon as possible to avoid payment delays.

### I received PM Kisan money by mistake. What should I do?

If you received PM Kisan money despite being ineligible (for example, you are a government employee or income tax payer), you are required to return the amount. The government conducts periodic verification and ineligible beneficiaries are asked to refund the money. You can voluntarily return it through the "Refund Online" option on the PM Kisan portal, or contact your local agriculture office. Not returning the money can result in recovery proceedings.

title: UPSC Eligibility 2026 - Age Limit, Qualification & Number
description: Complete guide to UPSC CSE 2026 eligibility covering age limits for all categories, educational qualification, number of attempts allowed, and special.
author: Mahitosh Dey
content:
## What is UPSC CSE?

The Union Public Service Commission Civil Services Examination, commonly known as UPSC CSE, is the gateway to India's most prestigious government positions. Through this single exam, candidates are selected for the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), Indian Foreign Service (IFS), Indian Revenue Service (IRS), and about 20 other All India and Central Services.

Every year, roughly 10 to 12 lakh candidates apply for UPSC CSE, making it one of the toughest competitive exams in the world. But before you start dreaming about becoming a District Collector or an Ambassador, the first thing you need to check is whether you are eligible to appear for this exam. The eligibility criteria cover your age, education, nationality, and the number of attempts you get.

I have seen many aspirants spend months preparing only to realise that they missed the age limit by a few months or did not understand the attempt rules properly. This guide covers every detail of UPSC CSE 2026 eligibility so you can plan accordingly. For more UPSC-related content, check out [UPSC jobs](/category/upsc) on our portal.

## Educational Qualification

### Degree Requirement

The basic educational qualification for UPSC CSE is a **Bachelor's degree from any recognised university**. The degree can be in any subject or stream — Arts, Science, Commerce, Engineering, Medicine, Law, or anything else. UPSC does not discriminate based on your field of study.

Here is what counts as a valid qualification:
- A Bachelor's degree (BA, B.Sc, B.Com, B.Tech, BBA, BCA, LLB, MBBS, etc.) from a university incorporated by an Act of the Central or State Legislature
- A degree from an institution recognised by UGC or AICTE
- A degree declared equivalent to a recognised university degree by a government order
- A professional or technical qualification recognised as equivalent to a Bachelor's degree by the government

### Can Final-Year Students Apply?

**Yes**, students who are appearing in the final year of their graduation can apply for UPSC CSE. If you have not received your degree but have appeared for the qualifying exam, you are eligible to appear for the Preliminary exam. However, you must produce proof of passing the degree before the Mains examination. If selected for Mains, you will need to submit your degree or provisional certificate.

### Distance Education and Open University Degrees

Degrees obtained through distance education or open universities are fully accepted as long as the university is recognised by UGC. IGNOU degrees, for example, are completely valid for UPSC. There is no difference in treatment between a regular degree and a distance degree for eligibility purposes.

## Age Limit

Age is one of the most critical eligibility factors for UPSC. Missing the upper age limit by even one day means you cannot appear, no matter how well-prepared you are.

### Age Limits by Category

| Category | Minimum Age | Maximum Age | Age as on |
|----------|-------------|-------------|-----------|
| General | 21 years | 32 years | 1st August 2026 |
| OBC (Non-Creamy Layer) | 21 years | 35 years | 1st August 2026 |
| SC / ST | 21 years | 37 years | 1st August 2026 |
| PwBD (General) | 21 years | 42 years | 1st August 2026 |
| PwBD (OBC) | 21 years | 45 years | 1st August 2026 |
| PwBD (SC/ST) | 21 years | 47 years | 1st August 2026 |

**How to calculate**: If you were born on or after 2nd August 1994, you are within the General category upper age limit for UPSC CSE 2026. If you were born on 1st August 1994 or earlier, you are overage.

### Additional Age Relaxations

- **Defence Services personnel** disabled in operations: 3 years (General), 6 years (OBC), 8 years (SC/ST)
- **Ex-Servicemen** including Commissioned Officers and ECOs: 5 years
- **Residents of Jammu & Kashmir** (who resided there from 1st January 1980 to 31st December 1989): 5 years

These relaxations are cumulative with category-based relaxations in some cases. Always check the official notification for the exact relaxation applicable to your category combination.

## Number of Attempts Allowed

The number of attempts is limited for most categories. Planning your attempts is crucial for a long-term UPSC strategy.

| Category | Maximum Attempts |
|----------|-----------------|
| General | 6 attempts |
| OBC (Non-Creamy Layer) | 9 attempts |
| SC / ST | Unlimited (until age limit) |
| PwBD (General) | 9 attempts |
| PwBD (OBC) | 9 attempts |
| PwBD (SC/ST) | Unlimited (until age limit) |

### What Counts as an Attempt?

This is something many candidates get confused about. **Appearing for the Preliminary exam counts as one attempt**. It does not matter whether you passed Prelims or not, whether you appeared for both papers or just one, or whether you scored zero marks. If you sat in the examination hall for even one paper of Prelims, that is one attempt used.

**Filling the application form alone does not count as an attempt** if you do not appear for the exam. So if you applied but could not go to the exam centre, your attempt is not wasted.

### Strategic Attempt Planning

For General category candidates with 6 attempts, here is a common approach:
- **Attempt 1-2**: Learn the process, understand the pattern, and identify weak areas
- **Attempt 3-4**: Peak preparation phase with maximum focus
- **Attempt 5-6**: Final serious attempts with complete revision

Many successful candidates clear the exam in their 3rd or 4th attempt. Do not panic if your first attempt does not work out.

## Nationality Requirements

To appear for UPSC CSE, you must be one of the following:
1. A **citizen of India**
2. A **subject of Nepal or Bhutan**
3. A **Tibetan refugee** who came to India before 1st January 1962 with the intention of permanently settling
4. A **person of Indian origin** who migrated from Pakistan, Burma, Sri Lanka, East African countries (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania), Zambia, Malawi, Zaire, Ethiopia, or Vietnam with the intention of permanently settling in India

For categories 2, 3, and 4, the candidate must have a certificate of eligibility issued by the Government of India. Also, candidates from Nepal and Bhutan and category 4 candidates are **not eligible for the IAS and IPS** — they can only be appointed to other services.

## Physical Standards

While UPSC does not have a physical test for most services, certain services like IPS, IRS (Customs), Railway Protection Force, and some others have specific physical standards:

- **IPS**: Minimum height 165 cm for men, 150 cm for women (with relaxations for certain categories)
- **Vision**: For IPS and some other services, a minimum vision standard is required. Candidates with vision defects may be declared unfit for certain services
- **General health**: All candidates must be in good physical and mental health. A medical examination is conducted before final appointment

For IAS and most other civil services, there are no specific height, weight, or physical fitness requirements beyond general good health.

## Key Points to Remember

Here are the most important things to keep in mind about UPSC eligibility:

1. **No minimum percentage** in graduation is required. Even a third-division pass is eligible.
2. **Any degree discipline** is accepted. You do not need a specific subject to appear for UPSC.
3. **Age relaxation is category-specific**. Make sure you have the correct category certificate.
4. **Attempts are precious**. Plan them wisely, especially if you are in the General category.
5. **Physical standards** apply only for specific services like IPS, not for all services.
6. **Nationality certificate** is needed for non-Indian citizens who are otherwise eligible.
7. **Check the notification every year**. While eligibility criteria remain largely the same, small changes can happen. Always refer to the latest official notification.
8. **EWS (Economically Weaker Sections)** candidates from the General category do not get age relaxation but get reservation benefits. The attempt limit remains 6.

**One last piece of advice**: Do not let eligibility doubts hold you back from starting preparation. If you have a graduation degree, are within the age limit, and have remaining attempts, you are eligible. Start preparing today. The UPSC journey is long, but it begins with knowing that you qualify.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is a degree from an open university valid for UPSC?

Yes, a degree from an open university like IGNOU, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Open University, or any other open university recognised by the UGC is valid for UPSC CSE. The key requirement is that the university must be recognised by the University Grants Commission. Distance learning and correspondence degrees are also accepted as long as the university has UGC recognition.

### What happens if I have exhausted all my UPSC attempts?

Once you exhaust all your allowed attempts, you cannot appear for UPSC CSE again regardless of your age. General category gets 6 attempts, OBC gets 9, and SC/ST have unlimited attempts until the age limit. There is no provision to get extra attempts. However, you can still explore other civil services exams at the state level (State PCS) which have separate attempt limits.

### Does appearing for UPSC Prelims count as an attempt?

Yes, appearing for the UPSC Preliminary exam counts as one attempt regardless of whether you qualify for Mains or not. Even if you just sit for Paper 1 of Prelims and leave it blank, it counts as an attempt. However, simply filling the application form without actually appearing for the exam does not count as an attempt. This distinction is important for managing your attempts wisely.

### Is there a minimum percentage required in graduation for UPSC?

No, UPSC does not require any minimum percentage in graduation. You just need to have a Bachelor's degree from a recognised university. Whether you passed with 40 percent or 90 percent, you are equally eligible. This is one of the most democratic aspects of the UPSC exam — your graduation marks have no bearing on your eligibility or selection.

### Can a person with a criminal record appear for UPSC?

There is no bar on appearing for the UPSC exam if you have a criminal record. However, at the time of final appointment, a thorough background verification is done. If you have been convicted of a serious criminal offence, your appointment may be denied. Minor offences or cases that were dismissed may not affect your candidature. Each case is evaluated individually during the verification process.

title: Ayushman Bharat Card 2026: How to Apply, Download & Use
description: Everything you need to know about the Ayushman Bharat card in 2026: how to check eligibility, apply for the card, download it online, and use it for free.
author: Mahitosh Dey
content:
---

Medical emergencies have a way of arriving without warning — and in India, a single major hospitalisation can wipe out years of savings. That's the exact problem **Ayushman Bharat** was built to solve.

If your family is eligible, you get **₹5 lakh per year in health coverage** — completely free. No premium. No paperwork at the hospital. Just walk in, show your card, and get treated.

But here's the problem: millions of eligible families still haven't claimed their card. Some don't know they qualify. Some got confused by the process and gave up. This guide will walk you through everything — checking eligibility, applying, downloading the card, and actually using it when you need it.

---

## What is Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY?

**Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY)** is the world's largest government-funded health insurance scheme. Launched in 2018, it provides:

- **₹5 lakh health cover** per family per year
- **Cashless treatment** at government and private empanelled hospitals
- Coverage for **1,929+ medical procedures** including surgery, ICU, chemotherapy, dialysis, and more
- **Pre and post hospitalisation** expenses covered (up to 3 days before and 15 days after)
- **No cap on family size** — the entire family is covered under one card
- **Portable across India** — use it in any empanelled hospital anywhere in the country

| Detail | Info |
|--------|------|
| **Annual Coverage** | ₹5 lakh per family |
| **Premium** | Zero — completely free for beneficiaries |
| **Beneficiaries** | ~55 crore people (about 12 crore families) |
| **Official Website** | pmjay.gov.in / beneficiary.nha.gov.in |
| **Helpline** | 14555 (toll-free) |

This is not a reimbursement scheme — you don't pay and claim later. Treatment is **cashless at the hospital** from day one.

---

## Who is Eligible for Ayushman Bharat?

Eligibility is based on the **Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) 2011** data and state government lists. You don't apply for eligibility — either your family is already in the list, or it isn't.

### Automatically Eligible (Rural Families)

If your family falls into any of these categories in the SECC data, you're likely eligible:

- Families with no permanent house (living in kutcha house with one room)
- Families with no adult member aged 16–59
- Female-headed households with no adult male member aged 16–59
- Families with a disabled member and no able-bodied adult earner
- SC/ST households
- Landless agricultural labourers with manual casual labour as primary income

### Automatically Eligible (Urban Families)

Urban workers in these occupations are covered:

- Rag pickers, beggars, domestic workers
- Street vendors, cobblers, hawkers
- Construction workers, plumbers, masons, painters
- Washermen, sanitation workers, sweepers
- Home-based artisans, handicraft workers
- Transport workers — drivers, conductors, helpers
- Shop workers, delivery assistants, peons, security guards

### Also Covered

- All **RSBY (Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana)** beneficiaries are included
- Many **state governments** have extended coverage beyond SECC — check your state's merged scheme (e.g., Maharashtra's Mahatma Jyotirao Phule Jan Arogya Yojana, Delhi's merged scheme)

---

## Step 1 — Check If You Are Eligible

Before applying for the card, first verify your eligibility.

**Online Method:**
1. Go to **pmjay.gov.in**
2. Click **"Am I Eligible?"**
3. Enter your mobile number → get OTP → verify
4. Enter your **State**, then search by:
   - Name + Date of Birth + Mobile
   - Name + Mobile Number
   - Name + Ration Card Number
   - RSBY URN Number
5. If your family is in the database, it will show your details

**By Calling:**
- Call **14555** (toll-free) and ask if your name is in the PM-JAY beneficiary list

**At the Hospital:**
- Any Ayushman Mitra (help desk) at an empanelled hospital can check your eligibility for free

If your name appears — great, move to the next step. If not, check whether your state has its own extended scheme that might cover you.

---

## Step 2 — How to Apply and Get the Ayushman Bharat Card

Getting the card is straightforward. You don't need to fill long forms or submit documents at a government office.

### Method 1 — Ayushman App (Easiest)

1. Download **"Ayushman App"** from the Google Play Store
2. Open the app → click **"Beneficiary"**
3. Log in with your **Aadhaar-linked mobile number**
4. Verify with OTP
5. Your family details and eligibility will appear
6. Select your name → click **"Download Card"**
7. Complete **eKYC** — either OTP-based (if mobile linked to Aadhaar) or face authentication via the app camera
8. Your Ayushman card is generated and ready to download

### Method 2 — Common Service Centre (CSC)

1. Visit your nearest **CSC / Jan Seva Kendra**
2. Carry: Aadhaar card + Ration card (if available) + Mobile number
3. The operator will verify your eligibility and complete biometric eKYC
4. The card is printed on the spot or sent to your registered mobile

### Method 3 — Empanelled Hospital Help Desk

Every empanelled hospital has an **Ayushman Mitra** — a dedicated help desk. You can:
1. Walk in and ask the Ayushman Mitra to check your eligibility
2. If eligible, they'll complete the eKYC and generate your card right there
3. This is particularly useful if you need treatment urgently and don't have the card yet

---

## Step 3 — How to Download Your Ayushman Card Online

If you're already registered and just need to download or reprint your card:

1. Go to **beneficiary.nha.gov.in**
2. Click **"Login"** → select **"Beneficiary"**
3. Enter your **Aadhaar-linked mobile number**
4. Verify with OTP
5. Your family member list will appear
6. Click on your name → **"Download Card"**
